In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no subtypes of ADHD.
ADHD is not a unitary disorder, but a syndrome of several different subtypes, with different genetic, neurobiological, and environmental risk factors.
the ADHD subtypes are different from each other in a number of aspects, but the severity differences are not that clear cut.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ADHD is a heterogeneous disorder with different subtypes that are associated with different risk factors.
we were able to identify a group of ADHD patients who have an earlier onset of the disorder, more comorbidity and more severe ADHD symptoms.

the results of the study are consistent with the idea that the ADHD subtypes are different from one another, but that the differences are not large enough to warrant a conclusion that the subtypes are different diseases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are differences in the clinical features and neurocognitive profile of the inattentive versus the hyperactive-impulsive subtype of ADHD.

there is a clear distinction between ADHD and ASD in the Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1986, and this distinction is evident in the early school years, even if the children have been identified by a multidisciplinary assessment team.
the ADHD subtypes, as defined by DSM-IV, are not valid, and should not be used in clinical practice or research.
